passage: Daniel had a lab shift until seven in Glasgow on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and Kwame worked evenings at a hotel in Accra on other days. For a month their calls had been random, one of them always tired or busy. On a Sunday morning they sat down, each with a paper calendar, and did it properly. "Tuesday at eight my time, after the lab. Friday at ten, before your shift." "And Sunday?" "Sunday is the long one. Two hours, no phones, no other tabs." They wrote it in permanent pen. That week Kwame's Tuesday call started at five past eight because a bus was late, and neither minded. On Sunday they talked for two hours and did not notice the light change.

qa.q: At what time on Tuesdays did Daniel and Kwame agree to call?
qa.a: They agreed to call at eight, Daniel's time, after the lab.

qa.q: What is Kwame feeling about the new arrangement?
qa.a: Kwame seems relieved and settled, since the calls no longer depend on who is tired, and the late bus does not bother anyone.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the couple add for a week when a call must be missed, and why?
qa.a: They could exchange a short voice message that day, because a small contact keeps the link alive when the live call cannot happen.

qa.q: How might Daniel see the long Sunday slot?
qa.a: Daniel gets two uninterrupted hours with no other tabs, which makes it feel like time set aside for the relationship and not squeezed between lab work.

grounding: Shows a couple fixing regular call times around lab hours and shifts, with one weekend slot kept for a long conversation.

passage: Sunday night, before the move. Amandeep and I finally had The Talk, by video, with tea on both sides. We had been guessing what the other expected, so I asked: "What do you actually need from me?" Amandeep said a quick message every day, even a boring one. And honesty about feelings, even when it is awkward. I said I need room during exams and I will not be able to talk much some weeks. We wrote it in a shared note under the heading "our rules, subject to change". Five lines. Amandeep added: "If one of us goes quiet, we ask, not assume." I feel lighter, like a knot loosened a little. Tomorrow I go. Not scared, just aware. — Kamal

qa.q: What heading did Kamal and Amandeep write on their note?
qa.a: They wrote the heading 'our rules, subject to change'.

qa.q: What is Kamal feeling at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Kamal feels lighter and calm, describing a knot that loosened a little, and aware rather than scared about the move.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the couple add after some months, and why?
qa.a: They could review the note together every few months, because needs change and a review keeps the rules from turning into old promises.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see the talk?
qa.a: Amandeep asks for a daily message and honesty and adds the rule about asking, so Amandeep seems to want closeness and clarity more than long calls.

grounding: Shows a couple discussing what each needs before a move and writing shared expectations, with a place for exam time.

subtype: Approach: assuming silence means loss of interest [Pitfall]
passage: Counsellor's note, written by Ms Fernandes. Joseph came on Monday, tired, phone in his hand. He explained that his girlfriend Jatin, in another city, had answered only twice in a week, during her exams. He had started imagining she had gone cold. He sent messages every hour: "Are you angry?", "Did I do something?" The last one at midnight. She replied, "I am studying, please stop," and they argued badly. Joseph said he felt ashamed afterwards. We sat together with a piece of paper and listed other reasons someone goes quiet in exam week. He wrote seven. I did not tell him what to do next. He decided to apologise and to ask, once, how she would like to stay in touch this fortnight.

qa.q: How many other reasons did Joseph write?
qa.a: Joseph wrote seven.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he sent messages every hour?
qa.a: Joseph was anxious and afraid Jatin had gone cold, and he felt ashamed afterwards when the argument came.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Joseph use during Jatin's exams, and why?
qa.a: Joseph could agree in advance on a message or two a day and wait, because a plan made in calm times keeps worry from pushing him into pressure.

qa.q: How might Jatin have felt when the messages kept coming?
qa.a: Jatin likely felt pressured and frustrated while studying, since she asked him to stop and an argument followed.

grounding: Shows a student reading a partner's slower replies during exams as lost interest, sending many anxious messages, and starting an argument.

subtype: Approach: emotion-aware planning before a hard call [Thinking]
passage: On the third Saturday morning, Sabina put down her phone and said to Gargi, over the video call, "Can we talk about our nights?" Gargi nodded. For weeks, the late calls had ended badly. They were both worn out after work, and anything serious, like money for the visit or who would move cities, ended in raised voices and a click of the phone. "It's not the topics," Sabina said. "It's the hour. At eleven I can barely think." So they made a plan. Serious things wait for Saturday mornings, with breakfast. Weeknights are light: what they ate, a funny thing at work, a song. The next Wednesday they talked about Gargi's neighbour's parrot for half an hour and both slept well.

qa.q: When did Sabina and Gargi decide to hold serious topics?
qa.a: They decided to hold serious topics for Saturday mornings, with breakfast.

qa.q: What is Sabina feeling about the late-night calls at the start of the scene?
qa.a: Sabina feels tired and frustrated by the fights, and says she can barely think at eleven.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the couple use if a serious matter cannot wait until Saturday, and why?
qa.a: They could send a short message asking to talk sooner at a calm time, because a request for a proper slot keeps the issue from being blurted out late at night.

qa.q: How does Gargi seem to see Sabina's proposal?
qa.a: Gargi nods and joins the plan without arguing, so Gargi seems relieved that the fights came from the hour and not from the relationship.

grounding: Shows a couple noticing that late-night calls turn into fights and moving heavy topics to a calmer weekend time.

passage: In the college library, Mehak stood at the window with her phone on video, while Mahima sat in a hostel room across the city. "Give me your dates." "Internals start on the ninth, finals on the twenty-second." Mehak typed both into a shared calendar in blue. "Mine are red. The fifth to the eighteenth." They looked at the screen: a solid block of colour. "So fewer calls those weeks. Two short ones?" "Two short ones, and no guilt." Mehak added a green star after the twenty-second: "Long call, no books." Mahima smiled at it. A student at the next table looked up, and Mehak lowered her voice, still smiling. That night neither wondered what a quiet day meant.

qa.q: What colour did Mehak use for Mahima's exam dates?
qa.a: Mehak used blue for Mahima's exam dates.

qa.q: What is Mahima feeling when she sees the green star?
qa.a: Mahima feels happy and reassured, smiling at the planned long call after the exams.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the couple add if one of them still worries during exam weeks, and why?
qa.a: They could agree on one short check-in message, because a small agreed signal covers the gap when full calls are paused.

qa.q: How might the student at the next table see Mehak on the phone?
qa.a: The student looks up at the voice in the library, so the student sees a person quietly having a personal call and not a distraction from work.

grounding: Shows a couple marking exam weeks on a shared calendar, agreeing on fewer calls then, and planning a longer catch-up afterward.

subtype: Approach: planning a visit with a shared budget [Action]
passage: Dilnaz and Hrithik sat over one spreadsheet, her in Mumbai, him in Pune, by video. Column A: train fare, both ways. Column B: two nights in a small guest house. Column C: food. Hrithik added: "That comes to about the same as a month of my allowance." "So we alternate. This visit I pay the train and you pay the stay. Next time swap." "Fair." Dilnaz added a line at the bottom: "Small tin, five hundred a month each, for visits only." They decided on the date, the 17th, because neither had a test. Hrithik looked at the sheet, and at her. "It's our first real plan." "It's a weekend," Dilnaz smiled. "But it's a start." She saved the file as "Visit 1".

qa.q: On which date did Dilnaz and Hrithik decide to meet?
qa.a: They decided on the 17th.

qa.q: What is Hrithik feeling when he calls it their first real plan?
qa.a: Hrithik feels moved and hopeful, looking at the sheet and at her as the visit becomes concrete.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the pair use if money gets tight, and why?
qa.a: They could plan a shorter or closer meeting or use an existing free day, because a smaller visit keeps the promise without straining either budget.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz see the visit plan?
qa.a: Dilnaz calls it just a weekend but a start, and saves the file as 'Visit 1', so she seems to treat it as the first of several trips.

grounding: Shows a couple planning a visit with costs written down, taking turns paying, and putting aside a small regular amount.

subtype: Approach: open-ended distance with no end date [Pitfall]
passage: Nkechi's last term in Lagos ended in four months. Kwame's programme in Toronto had a year left. They talked every night, cheerful and sweet, about films, families, and food. Neither said the word "after". Once Kwame started: "When you finish, do you..." and Nkechi said quickly, "Let's not spoil tonight." The silence that followed was a small stone. The next month it got bigger. Nkechi began to answer late. Kwame started to sound careful. Each privately guessed what the other would say, and each guess was worse than the truth might have been. By the third month, their conversations were shorter and politer. In the fourth month, an argument about a delayed message ended with "You never plan anything", and the real subject was still unspoken.

qa.q: How many months did Nkechi have left in Lagos?
qa.a: Nkechi had four months left.

qa.q: What was Nkechi feeling when Kwame began the sentence 'When you finish, do you...'?
qa.a: Nkechi felt afraid of the answer and wanted to protect the evening, so the subject was cut off quickly.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the couple use, and why?
qa.a: They could set a calm time to talk about where each would live after graduation, because leaving it unspoken let hope turn into guesses.

qa.q: How might Kwame see Nkechi's late answers?
qa.a: Kwame sounds careful and guesses at the reason, so Kwame may read the delay as distance without knowing the real fear behind it.

grounding: Shows a couple with no end date who never discuss where they will live afterwards, so unspoken fear turns hope into resentment.

subtype: Approach: contingency planning for career moves [Thinking]
passage: Anjali, you asked how we handle the job question, so I'll tell you, I'm Ramesh. Last month I got an interview in Hyderabad. Anjali is here, in Pune, on her third year. We could not decide anything, only worry. So one evening we did something different. We wrote three futures on a page. One: I get the job and move. Two: Anjali gets an offer somewhere else. Three: both stay put. For each we asked what we would do for the first year. Not promises, just options: visits every six weeks, a review call after each result. We agreed to look at the page again in March. I thought it would be dry. It felt kind, honestly. Every future had a way through, and none needed a promise tonight.

qa.q: In which month did Ramesh and Anjali agree to look at the page again?
qa.a: They agreed to look at the page again in March.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling before the page was written?
qa.a: Ramesh was worried and stuck, since they could not decide anything and only worried.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the pair add, and why?
qa.a: They could learn about the real costs and timelines of each city, because a plan for a future is stronger with facts than with guesses.

qa.q: How might Anjali see the page of three futures?
qa.a: Anjali is one of the people in the futures and helps fill them in, so she likely sees a way to talk about the job without being asked to promise.

grounding: Shows a couple thinking through several possible futures and agreeing when to revisit without forcing any promise.

subtype: Approach: revising the routine when it feels forced [Revision]
passage: Francis, you look tired of your nightly calls, so let me, Ujjwal, tell you about mine. My wife and I were apart for two years when I worked on a ship. In the beginning we called every night, no matter what. By the ninth month we were both doing it like homework. "How was your day?" "Fine. And yours?" Ten minutes of nothing, then sleep. One evening she said, "Do we even enjoy this?" We laughed, because it was true. We changed the rule. Short messages every day: a photo of tea, a line from a song. Two real calls each week, with no phone in the other hand. The relationship felt light again, and calls became something to look forward to.

qa.q: How many real calls each week did Ujjwal and Ujjwal's wife keep?
qa.a: They kept two real calls each week.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling by the ninth month of nightly calls?
qa.a: Ujjwal was bored and dutiful, treating the calls like homework rather than a joy.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned things around, and why?
qa.a: They admitted together that the calls felt like a chore and changed the rule, because honesty allowed a lighter routine that they actually wanted.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal's wife have felt when she asked if they even enjoyed it?
qa.a: She was probably tired of the routine too but worried about saying it, and the shared laugh shows relief at finding both felt the same.

grounding: Shows a couple revising a call routine that had become a chore, switching to short daily messages and two proper calls each week.

subtype: Approach: ending it kindly after honest reflection [Revision]
passage: Kunal, you asked me how I knew it was time, so let old Kashish tell you. Rohan and I, we were together in college and then apart in different cities for a year. We talked, properly, more than once. I wanted to start a business at home. Rohan wanted a research career abroad. Each time we found a way to say "we can manage", and each time it felt more like a sentence to repeat than a promise. One evening I said, "I think the distance isn't working, and I think it's because we want different lives." Rohan was quiet, then said, "I've been thinking the same." We cried a little. We agreed to be kind, to say a proper goodbye, and to write in a year. It hurt. It was also clean.

qa.q: How long had Kashish and Rohan been in different cities?
qa.a: They had been in different cities for a year.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when saying the words about the distance?
qa.a: Kashish was sad and unsure but honest, since the words came after many talks and ended in a little crying.

qa.q: What choice inside the story kept the parting respectful, and why?
qa.a: Kashish said the truth plainly and asked to be kind and say goodbye properly, because a clear honest ending left less room for blame.

qa.q: How might Rohan have felt on hearing it?
qa.a: Rohan was quiet, then said the same thing had been on Rohan's mind, which suggests relief mixed with sadness that Kashish spoke first.

grounding: Shows ending a long-distance relationship kindly after repeated honest conversations about different goals.
